```{r}
#| label: prerequisites
#| include: false
has_ggally   <- requireNamespace("GGally", quietly = TRUE)
has_penguins <- requireNamespace("palmerpenguins", quietly = TRUE)
source(here::here("comprehensive_exam/numerical_tie_attempts/pcp_spread_ties.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(ggpcp)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

## Why ties on numeric axes are a problem

The `iris` flowers were measured to the nearest millimetre.
On petal width, 150 flowers take 22 distinct values, and 148 of them share
their value with another flower. In a parallel coordinate plot, 150 lines pass
through 22 points on that axis. A line enters a point, several lines leave it,
and nothing in the plot says which one to follow.

A parallel coordinate plot promises that an observation can be followed from
axis to axis. At a tie the promise breaks: the tie is a fork in the road.

`pcp_spread_ties()` repairs it. Every tied observation gets its own place on
the axis, inside a band no taller than the grid on which the variable was
measured, and ordered so that lines do not cross inside the band.

This vignette is for the analyst whose numeric variables are counts, scores,
or measurements recorded on a grid, and who today chooses between overlapping
lines and turning the variable into a factor.

### Where the published pipeline stops

`ggpcp` separates the data wrangling for a parallel coordinate plot from its
rendering. Three steps prepare the data -- `pcp_select()`, `pcp_scale()` and
`pcp_arrange()` -- and the last of these breaks ties on **categorical** axes:
observations sharing the same level are spread out evenly and ordered by their
values on the neighbouring axes, so that every observation can be followed
through the plot.

Numeric axes get no such treatment, and they carry ties too. Measurements are
recorded at a finite resolution, counts and scores take only a handful of
values, and discretized variables are often kept numeric so that their order
and spacing are preserved. Wherever several observations share a value, their
line segments meet in a single point on the axis and fan out again on either
side. These *bow-ties* hide how many observations the point stands for and
which incoming segment continues as which outgoing one.

Petal width is the worst case in `iris`, not the only one: all four
measurements are recorded to the nearest 0.1 cm, so each axis has only 22 to
43 distinct values for 150 flowers.

```{r}
#| label: fig-iris-before
#| fig-cap: "iris with ties broken on the factor axis only: every numeric axis shows bow-ties where observations share a value."
iris_pcp <- iris %>%
  pcp_select(Sepal.Length:Species) %>%
  pcp_scale() %>%
  pcp_arrange("from-right")        # breaks ties on the factor axis

iris_pcp %>%
  ggplot(aes_pcp()) +
  geom_pcp_axes() +
  geom_pcp(aes(colour = Species), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_pcp_boxes() +
  geom_pcp_labels() +
  theme_pcp()
```

## `pcp_spread_ties()`: a fourth data wrangling step

The categorical step stops where the numeric axes begin. `pcp_spread_ties()`
adds a step to the pipeline that picks up there. It is placed after
`pcp_arrange()` and uses the same vocabulary for its `method` argument.

```{r}
#| label: fig-iris-after
#| fig-cap: "The same data after `pcp_spread_ties(\"from-right\", sigma = 0.9)`: each tied value occupies a band of height $\\delta_j$, ordered by the axis to the right."
iris_ties <- iris_pcp %>%
  pcp_spread_ties("from-right", sigma = 0.9, min_gap = 0)

iris_ties %>%
  ggplot(aes_pcp()) +
  geom_pcp_axes() +
  geom_pcp(aes(colour = Species), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_pcp_boxes() +
  geom_pcp_labels() +
  theme_pcp()
```

Every tied value now occupies a small band on the axis. Within a band the
observations are ordered by their position on the neighbouring axis (to the
right, for `"from-right"`), which untangles the segments between the two axes
in the same way `pcp_arrange()` does for factor variables. (The `min_gap = 0`
argument silences a diagnostic warning that is discussed in @sec-diagnostics.)

### How the bands are built

Jitter would also separate the lines, but at random, and by a width that means
nothing in the data. The algorithm here, called *tie spread*, anchors the
bands at the resolution of the data instead:

1. **Resolution.** For every numeric axis the resolution $\delta_j$ is the
   smallest difference between two distinct (scaled) values on that axis.
   For `Sepal.Length`, for example, $\delta_j$ corresponds to 0.1 cm.
2. **Band.** A tied value $v$ is given the band
   $[\max(0, v - \delta_j/2),\ \min(1, v + \delta_j/2)]$. Bands of
   neighbouring values therefore touch but never overlap, and a value keeps
   its vertical position: an observation never moves closer to a different
   value than to its own.
3. **Margins.** A fraction `sigma` of each band is used for placing the
   observations; the remaining $(1 - \sigma)$ is split into two margins so
   that adjacent bands stay visually separate.
4. **Order and spacing.** The $k$ tied observations are placed at equal
   spacing across the inner region, ordered by their (already adjusted)
   position on the reference axis.

The axes are processed in a single sweep. For `"from-right"` the rightmost
axis is processed first and every other axis references the axis to its right;
`"from-left"` mirrors this. `"from-both"` starts at a `center` axis and moves
outward, with each axis referencing its neighbour closer to the center. The
first axis of the sweep has no reference axis; its ties are spread in the order
of the rows of the data, or in the order of a nominated neighbour
(`center_reference`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-from-both
#| fig-cap: "`from-both`, starting at `Petal.Length` and seeding its within-band order from `Petal.Width`."
iris_pcp %>%
  pcp_spread_ties("from-both", center = "Petal.Length",
                  center_reference = "Petal.Width", min_gap = 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes_pcp()) +
  geom_pcp_axes() +
  geom_pcp(aes(colour = Species), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_pcp_boxes() +
  geom_pcp_labels() +
  theme_pcp()
```

### One call for both variable types

Most data have ties of both kinds. `pcp_arrange_unified()` runs
`pcp_arrange()` and `pcp_spread_ties()` in one go
and is a drop-in replacement for `pcp_arrange()`:

```{r}
#| label: unified
#| eval: false
iris %>%
  pcp_select(Sepal.Length:Species) %>%
  pcp_scale() %>%
  pcp_arrange_unified("from-right", sigma = 0.9)
```

## The separation parameter `sigma`

A band filled to its edges touches its neighbours, and two tied values read as
one. `sigma` controls how much of each band is used for the observations.
Values close to 1 fill the band almost completely and the gaps between adjacent
bands shrink; smaller values leave wider gaps and tighter bundles.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sigma
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "Smaller `sigma` leaves wider gaps between bands and tighter bundles inside them."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "sigma = 0.5"
#|   - "sigma = 0.9"
#| layout-ncol: 2
for (s in c(0.5, 0.9)) {
  p <- iris_pcp %>%
    pcp_spread_ties("from-right", sigma = s, min_gap = 0) %>%
    ggplot(aes_pcp()) +
    geom_pcp_axes() +
    geom_pcp(aes(colour = Species), alpha = 0.6) +
    theme_pcp() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
  print(p)
}
```

## Spreading only some axes

Not every axis needs spreading. A near-continuous variable has no ties to
break, and a variable with a handful of levels is better served as a factor
(see the flea example below). The `vars` argument restricts the spreading to a
selection of axes. It takes a tidyselect specification, as `pcp_select()`
does: bare names, positions, selector functions such as `starts_with()`, or a
character vector. Axes that are not selected -- and factor axes in general --
are left untouched.

```{r}
#| label: fig-vars
#| fig-cap: "Only the two width axes are spread (`vars = ends_with(\"Width\")`)."
iris_pcp %>%
  pcp_spread_ties("from-right", vars = ends_with("Width"), min_gap = 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes_pcp()) +
  geom_pcp_axes() +
  geom_pcp(aes(colour = Species), alpha = 0.6) +
  theme_pcp()
```

## Annotating the bands

Spreading moves observations off their values, and the reader should be told
so. A box around the band is the cue: positions inside it are spread for
legibility, not because the values differ.

The geometry of every band is stored in the attribute `"pcp_ties"` of the
result. `pcp_tie_boxes()` turns it into a data frame of rectangles and
`geom_pcp_tieboxes()` draws them, mirroring `geom_pcp_boxes()` and
`geom_pcp_labels()` for factor axes. A rectangle covers the inner region of its
band, where the observations sit, so boxes at neighbouring values stay apart;
`extent = "band"` draws the full band instead. The labels show the original tied values,
which are recovered from the `pcp_level` column of the data. With
`labels = TRUE` a count label, `n = k`, is also placed beside every box that
holds at least `count_min_n` observations (three by default); `counts = FALSE`
leaves it out. The boxes should be added *before* `geom_pcp()` so that they
sit behind the lines, and `min_n` suppresses boxes for small bands. To draw
the labels in front of the lines, add them in a second call after
`geom_pcp()` with `box = FALSE`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-boxes
#| fig-cap: "Tie bands with at least eight observations, annotated with the original tied value."
head(attr(iris_ties, "pcp_ties"))

boxes <- pcp_tie_boxes(iris_ties, boxwidth = 0.2, min_n = 8)

iris_ties %>%
  ggplot(aes_pcp()) +
  geom_pcp_tieboxes(boxes, labels = TRUE) +
  geom_pcp_axes() +
  geom_pcp(aes(colour = Species), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_pcp_boxes() +
  geom_pcp_labels() +
  theme_pcp()
```

## Diagnostics {#sec-diagnostics}

The method has two limits, and the function reports both rather than drawing
a plot that will be misread. `pcp_spread_ties()` warns:

* when the gap between adjacent bands, $(1 - \sigma)\delta_j$, is smaller than
  `min_gap` (0.005 of the axis by default), adjacent bands may visually merge
  -- a smaller `sigma`, or fewer displayed values, helps;
* when the spacing between tied observations inside a band falls below
  `min_spacing` (0.001 by default), the band is saturated and individual
  observations will overplot.

For `iris` the first warning fires on every axis with the default settings:
the measurements are fine-grained relative to their range, so $\delta_j$ is
small. The warning can be acknowledged by lowering `min_gap`, as in the
examples above, or avoided by choosing a smaller `sigma`.

```{r}
#| label: warnings
res <- iris_pcp %>% pcp_spread_ties("from-right")
```

## Numeric ties versus converting to a factor

Converting a numeric variable to a factor is the obvious way to break its
ties, and `pcp_arrange()` already supports it. Sometimes it is the right way.

The package README treats the `aede2` variable of the `flea` data (a front
angle recorded in steps of 7.5 degrees) by turning it into a factor. The
variable takes nine evenly spaced values, so little is lost: the levels keep
their order, and the box heights show how many beetles share each angle. For a
variable with a handful of levels, the factor remains the treatment to use.

The other measurements are a different case. `tars1` takes 46 distinct values
for 74 beetles. As a factor it becomes a ladder of 46 thin boxes, and the
metric scale is gone: the beetle at 242, 19 units above its nearest neighbour,
sits one rung above it like every other beetle. `pcp_spread_ties()` keeps such
a variable numeric, so the distances between values stay on the axis while the
bands make the ties traceable.

The two treatments combine in one plot. Below, `aede2` is converted to a
factor, and `pcp_arrange_unified()` arranges it and spreads the ties on the
remaining numeric axes in the same call. `head`, with 13 values, sits at the
boundary, where either treatment is defensible; it is kept numeric here.

```{r}
#| label: fig-flea
#| eval: !expr has_ggally
#| fig-cap: "flea: `aede2` as a factor, the other five measurements kept numeric with ties spread and annotated; `species` appears on both ends."
data(flea, package = "GGally")

flea_ties <- flea %>%
  mutate(aede2 = factor(aede2)) %>%    # few levels: break its ties as a factor
  pcp_select(species, 2:7, species) %>%
  pcp_scale() %>%
  pcp_arrange_unified("from-right", min_gap = 0)

flea_boxes <- pcp_tie_boxes(flea_ties, boxwidth = 0.15, min_n = 3)

flea_ties %>%
  ggplot(aes_pcp()) +
  geom_pcp_tieboxes(flea_boxes, labels = TRUE) +
  geom_pcp_axes() +
  geom_pcp(aes(colour = species), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_pcp_boxes(boxwidth = 0.15) +
  geom_pcp_labels() +
  theme_pcp()
```

## Penguins

The penguins put both limits of the method on one plot. Integer-valued
measurements such as flipper length and body mass create frequent ties in the
`palmerpenguins` data. The unified call treats the factor axes and the numeric
axes together. Body mass is recorded in steps of 25 g over a range of 3600 g,
so its resolution $\delta_j$ is tiny and bands with many observations become
saturated -- the second diagnostic warning reports which values are affected.
The bands still mark where the ties are; they can no longer show each bird.

```{r}
#| label: fig-penguins
#| eval: !expr has_penguins
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "penguins: factor and numeric ties treated in one call; boxes shown for bands of at least eight birds."
data(penguins, package = "palmerpenguins")

peng_ties <- penguins %>%
  na.omit() %>%
  pcp_select(bill_length_mm:body_mass_g, island, species) %>%
  pcp_scale() %>%
  pcp_arrange_unified("from-right", sigma = 0.9, min_gap = 0)

peng_boxes <- pcp_tie_boxes(peng_ties, boxwidth = 0.15, min_n = 8)

peng_ties %>%
  ggplot(aes_pcp()) +
  geom_pcp_tieboxes(peng_boxes, labels = TRUE) +
  geom_pcp_axes() +
  geom_pcp(aes(colour = species), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_pcp_boxes() +
  geom_pcp_labels() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#CC79A7", "#009E73")) +
  theme_pcp() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

## In short

- **A handful of levels:** convert the variable to a factor and let
  `pcp_arrange()` break its ties.
- **Many values with scattered ties:** keep the variable numeric and use
  `pcp_spread_ties()`.
- **No ties:** do nothing.

`pcp_arrange_unified()` and `vars` let one plot hold all three.

## Reference

Bradford D. (2026). *A Grammar of Graphics Approach to Managing Numerical
Ties in Parallel Coordinate Plots.*
